catalog_quote: Every noun contains one stress/tone syllable, usually in the word final position. Stress itself does not seem to be the most important consideration, but is more a result of emphasizing the particular word tone. The stress/tone syllable manifest either high (/), mid (-), or low (\) tone as shown in (24). 24) a. [oka] 'black bird' b. [oka] 'flying fox' c. [oka] 'black type of soil' ... Unstressed syllables either manifest a mid tone or the same tone as the stressed syllable. This produces rising and falling tone patterns in some words but the changes in pattern do not seem to indicate additional tonemes, as no contrast has been found. ... When a noun is affixed with any number of affixes the original tone and stress pattern remains on the noun itself. The affixation is always mid tone after a high or mid noun word final syllable, and low or mid after a noun word final low tone ... Verb s…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the held at the stated lines (318-453, §3 'Stress and tone'); the supplementary locators (§1.2 l.204-220, §4 l.707) also check out. Only nit: the ms's own pagination puts §3 on pp. 6-8 rather than 5-7. (2) Deciding source: an unpublished 19-pp SIL-PNG phonology ms (1995, rev. 2009) by the long-term resident fieldworkers. sources.citation: Anderson, Carol. 2010. Beginning Folopa Language Lessons and Simple Glossary. Ukarumpa: SIL-PNG. Ms., 109 pp. (SIL Language & Culture Archives item 41086; Glottolog ref 313766)
sources.quote: p.7-8: 'Some words in Folopa are pronounced exactly the same but have a different meaning. On some of those words there is a difference only in the tone, or pitch ... yia (high tone) mosquito / yia (low tone) fish; boką (high tone) black bird / boką (mid tone) large bat / boką (low tone) type of dark soil. All Folopa words have a pattern of tone and stress. ... In general, the important tone stress is on the last syllable of a basic word. A basic word is one without any added suffixes. When suffixes are added to nouns the tone and stress does not change. It still occurs on the last syllable of
sources.locator: 'Stress and Tone', pp. 7-8 (txt lines 320-356); also p. 5 (aa sequence) and p. 12 (kale 'stress on first syllable')
sources.note: fetched sources now; pp. 7-8 restate the analysis in plain terms (tone/pitch minimal triplets; 'important tone stress is on the last syllable of a basic word'; noun suffixes do not move it, verb suffixes attract it) and the glossary marks lexical tone on pairs. Confirms the record; could be added as a second citation.

sources.citation: MacDonald, George E. 1973. The Teberan language family. In Karl J. Franklin (ed.), The linguistic situation in the Gulf District and adjacent areas, Papua New Guinea (Pacific Linguistics C-26), 111-148. Canberra: ANU. (Glottolog ref 8971)
sources.quote: p.129: 'It is suspected that further investigation would reveal the presence of phonemic tone in Polopa. One example is AUR and BOR yá fish vs. ya mosquito.' p.133: 'Tone is common to Daribi, Polopa, Pawaia and Witu, but is not apparent in neighboring groups.' No statement on stress placement (survey wordlist data only).
sources.locator: §3.41 Polopa phonology, p. 129; §3.51 summary, p. 133 (txt lines 684-731, 971-973)
sources.note: fetched sources now; survey-level independent note that phonemic tone is suspected in Polopa (yá 'fish' vs ya 'mosquito', the same pair Anderson cites) and that tone is areal (Daribi, Polopa, Pawaia, Witu). Silent on stress placement; corroborates the tonal classification only.
